extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing papers, expositions, and books (graduate students, researchers, textbook authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on writing and presenting mathematical and computer-science research and expository papers and books, covering exposition, style, examples, notation, publishing strategy, and ethical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the reader's attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs are methods of getting readers' attention immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: titles like 'Trisecting the Angle, the Heptagon, and the Triskaidecagon', opening lines such as 'Can a graph be continuous and discontinuous?', and autobiographical openings that show immediate fascination. Being famous helps but good openings matter regardless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put everything up front (tell readers plainly what you will do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your readers in plain English what you are going to write about and let them decide whether they are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You can quintuple your readership if you will let them in on what it is that you are doing." Be explicit about goals/results early so readers can decide to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make results easy to find (readers scan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers scan papers looking for statements of theorems; summarize results using boldface or other emphasis so skimmers can latch on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop notational abbreviations and convoluted references in theorem statements; use boldface (or neon) for main results so 'page flippers' can make an informed decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep notation out of theorem statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid heavy notation or abbreviations in the statements of theorems; present them in accessible/plain language where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notational abbreviations and convoluted references make theorems hard to scan; state theorems in clear language and relegate heavy notation to surrounding discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motivation sparingly and effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide little motivation — enough to orient but not so much that readers lose the thread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few motivating examples (including ones that don't yield desired results) can be useful, but overuse of such negative examples loses charm and can annoy readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and puzzles to build intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Present examples or a mathematical puzzle before technical development to build the right mental structures in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example-before-algorithm technique helps readers see the non-triviality of a problem and primes them for the algorithm/proof. Beware of overuse and of introducing mysteriously convenient starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance chattiness and leanness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be chatty around proofs (motivation, intuition) but write the proofs themselves in a 'lean and mean' rigorous style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: aim to be chatty leading up to a proof, prove it concisely (Rudin-style), then be chatty afterwards. Adjust style over time as you gain confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend formal and informal exposition appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a mix of formal discussion and informal explanation with well-chosen examples for difficult/new areas; typographic conventions can help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nilsson & Genesereth chapter praised for blending formal/informal discussion and using a 'typewriter' font for logic. Choose conventions that clarify rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep definitions close to uses; repeat when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Place definitions near their first use and don't be ashamed to repeat definitions to aid reader comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defining something in Chapter 2 and first using it in Chapter 5; readers do not work like that. Repetition is acceptable to keep exposition clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself in the reader's place
rubrics_metrics.description: Write from the reader's perspective: remember what was hard to learn and order exposition accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend a day reading about a topic and write it up in the evening to get expository order right; advantage over experts is remembering common stumbling blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lots of good examples
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as too many examples; even simple examples convey much of an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple example can get three-quarters of an idea across; refine later with complex examples that show 'grubbies'. Finding examples that illustrate only the intended points takes time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter idiosyncrasies via co-authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authors help filter out author idiosyncrasies and improve the book's quality, even if they don't save time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff Ullman: co-authors don't save time but prevent 'craziness' that can make a book a dud; a small improvement over competitors can capture large market share.

rubrics_metrics.name: State types and use precise referential language
rubrics_metrics.description: State the types of your variables and avoid non-referential or vague words (e.g., non-referential 'this').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk about 'the set S' not 'S'; Jeff's English professor advised never to use the non-referential 'this' because it often leaves readers bewildered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify use of powerful machinery; keep level accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: If using advanced techniques, justify them and keep the exposition at a level readers can understand; avoid spending excessive space developing machinery if not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoff example: spend 20 pages teaching asymptotic analysis or refer and only do basic calculations. In general, keep exposition level down so readers can follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and metaphor cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analogy, metaphor, and simile where they will genuinely help readers understand but avoid forcing them when the subject resists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff: physics texts use analogy more; encourage analogy when you're sure the reader will get the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider naming and terminology carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology and names matter; choose them thoughtfully because names can stick and affect perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Daemon' vs 'Oracle', LR(k) vs L(k) grammars; community polls can change terminology (NP-complete example). Authors sometimes regret earlier naming choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match presentation to target journal type
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between research journals (require new, important, significant results) and expository journals (value excellent exposition); adjust presentation accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal of Algorithms accepts new/important/significant results and allows some leeway on presentation; The American Mathematical Monthly is expository and rewards clarity and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing for bad reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write papers to pad a publication list or merely to appear in a specific conference; those motives often produce sloppy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie Lamport: quality should trump quantity; integrity should police authors when external incentives do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism; cite and quote explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lift text or equations verbatim without clear quotation or attribution; imitation becomes culpable when a reasonable person would suspect copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prentice-Hall guidance: you can't copyright ideas but can copyright expression. Jeff's examples show near-verbatim quotation and identical typographic choices as suspicious. Be explicit when quoting; survey papers may quote more but should make attribution clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan book-market strategy and production practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing books, know the market, pick a niche (hardest/easiest/best), aim for substantial sales, and use production tactics to improve royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets: aim for ~10,000 domestic sales (e.g., 2,000/year for five years). Negotiate royalties (15% standard; can be doubled for high-sales expectations). Prepare camera-ready copy to reduce publisher costs and increase leverage. Choose a young/booming field if seeking large sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use second editions strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish new editions roughly every five years to reset the sales clock and renew revenue; earlier examples speed subsequent editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second editions still take significant time (~a kilohour), but reusing previous material makes them faster and financially valuable because buyers age out of earlier editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting/combinatorial results should yield integers
rubrics_metrics.description: When deriving counting formulas, ensure the final expression is an integer; integer-ness can reveal number-theoretic facts (e.g., Fermat's little theorem as a corollary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: combinatorial formulas must give integer answers; if they don't look integer, that's a signal of interesting mathematics. Use combinatorial reasoning to check divisibility/integrality properties.
